2860.heavy: 'palabras terminadas en consonante, en vocal con saltillo o en vocal con jota' = a word-final closed syllable: final consonant (postvocalic u /w/ counts as a consonant, §1.4 and §1.5), vowel + glottal stop ('saltillo'), vowel + j [h]. 2860.prule: Right-edge, coda-sensitive: stress the final syllable if the word ends in a consonant (postvocalic u = /w/ counts as a consonant), in vowel + glottal stop (saltillo) or in vowel + j [h]; otherwise (word ends in a plain vowel, short or long) stress the penultimate syllable. Future-tense suffix -ám carries the stress; in other tenses the root is stressed.

tn.quote: Il y a deux tons fondamentaux ou tonèmes: ton bas (a) et ton haut (á) . En principe, chaque syllabe de chaque élément a son ton propre et constant (ton lexical fixe) . Ainsi la mélodie de mots comme útundúkamba … tons inhérents à chacun des éléments constitutifs … Quand deux voyelles à ton différent sont réalisées en une syllabe, leurs tons sont représentés par un ton composé soit montant (a - á: ă) soit descendant (á - a: â); parfois même trois tons sont représentés
tn.translation: There are two fundamental tones or tonemes: low tone (a) and high tone (á). In principle, each syllable of each element has its own constant tone (fixed lexical tone). Thus the melody of words like útundúkamba … tones inherent in each of the constituent elements … When two vowels of different tone are realised in one syllable, their tones are represented by a compound tone, either rising (a-á: ă) or falling (á-a: â); sometimes even three tones are represented
tn.cite: Meeussen, A. E. 1952. Esquisse de la langue ombo (Maniema-Congo belge). Annales du Musée royal du Congo belge, Série in-8°, Sciences de l'homme, Linguistique 4. Tervuren: Musée royal du Congo belge. 44 pp.
tn.note: Two tonemes, low and high, fixed on every syllable; contours only as compounds on fused vowels; a light non-distinctive penultimate intensity accent that tends to attach to a high tone.

2864.prule: Primary word stress on the penultimate syllable of the word, whatever its length and irrespective of vowel length (quantity-insensitive); one main stress per word; a word-final V.V sequence is two syllables, so the first of the two vowels is stressed (kitlalía).
2864.srule: Long words may have secondary stresses ('puede tener acentos secundarios'); their placement is not given; the word has a single strong (main) stress.
2864.quote: La acentuación del náhuatl es casi siempre penúltima (grave), es decir se acentúa la sílaba anterior a la última de la palabra. When two or more syllables are suffixed to a root, the penultimate syllable receives primary stress and the root retains secondary stress. [Section 2 treats sentence intonation separately: 'There is often a rise on the stressed syllable (which is usually penultimate) and a great…
2869.dloc: Section 4 'Stress', rules 4.1-4.2, pp. 32-33; also section 2 p. 30, section 9.2.2 p. 42 ('Roots of more than one syllable have stress on their penultimate syllable', [hilgúki]) and section 9.3 p. 44 ('single-syllable roots, which always retain at least secondary stress'), endnotes 8-9 p. 55; cross-check Fields 1997 p. 239
2869.prule: Stress is non-phonemic (predictable). Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word ROOT; a root followed by one monosyllabic suffix keeps its root stress (surface word-antepenult for a disyllabic root, e.g. /bó.ton-.gwek/ 'she lied'); when two or more syllables are suffixed, primary stress moves to the penultimate syllable of the whole word and the root retains secondary stress (e.g. /bó.ton-.gwé.ka/ 'he lied': underline = primary on gwé, acute kept on the root syllable = retained secondary stress). Bare roots therefore surface as penultimate; the author summarises the system as penultimate ('usually penultimate' 1991:30; 'Orya is pronounced with penultimate stress' 1997:239). Rule 4.2 (segmental, not weight): primary stress always precedes a cluster of two sonorant consonants (/n/, /m/, /ŋ/, /l/) when that cluster is on the penult or antepenult; it overrides 4.1 when a monosyllabic suffix creates such a cluster (/túmbuŋ-na/ -> [tũmbṹŋnu] 'round (FOC)', /yóhan-mo/ -> [yohã́nmo] 'Yohan's') and can turn normal penultimate stress into antepenultimate (/bálk-gul.lá.da/ -> [balkgúluda] 'he caught her'); a cluster farther from the word end than the antepenult leaves the stress unchanged.
2869.srule: Root secondary stress (morphological, not rhythmic): when two or more syllables are suffixed and primary stress moves to the word penult, the root retains secondary stress on its own stressed syllable (root penult, or the sole syllable of a monosyllabic root), e.g. /bó.ton-.gwé.ka/ 'he lied', /en.lá.la-.gwe.bíl.nan/ 'I've been thinking about it'; 'Roots retain secondary stress' (p. 42); single-syllable roots 'always retain at least secondary stress' (p. 44). No alternating/rhythmic secondary stresses are described.

2874.dq: Stress in Otuho is very indistinct, and many words do not have a stressed syllable. A strong consonant often gives greater stress to the syllable in which it occurs. A neutral consonant may be strongly articulated when the word in which it occurs is being emphasised, producing the same phonetic result as a strong consonant, i.e. a stressed syllable.

2874.prule: No phonemic word stress. Stress is 'very indistinct'; many words have no stressed syllable; where a syllable sounds stressed this is a phonetic by-product of a strong (fortis) onset consonant (t, k, d, r, w:, l:, y:, s, n: per Chart 4) or of emphatic articulation of a neutral consonant. Muratori's claimed stress minimal pair ('ojo 'said' vs o'jo 'with') is reanalysed as a tone contrast. Tone is phonemic with lexical and grammatical functions: three or four level tones plus rising and falling glides. No positional stress rule is given anywhere in the article.

2876.dq: Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic—a word may consist of one or one and a half syllables. In the latter case a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable, a structurally impoverished unit that is constructed from a restricted set of segments.
2876.dloc: Sidwell & Jacq 2003 sec. 4.2 'PWB phonological word', p.33; Oi profile sec. 3.7 'Oi (also Oy, Oey)', pp.26-28, stress-relevant sentence p.28. Daniell 2020 p.4 sec. 3.1 'Nasal minor syllables'
2876.prule: Stress falls on the word-final main syllable. A phonological word is one syllable or one and a half syllables (minor syllable + main syllable); when a minor syllable is present it is a structurally reduced, unstressed unit (restricted onset set, epenthetic [a]/schwa-like vowel, optional nasal/rhotic coda) and the following main syllable is stressed. Non-contrastive, computable from syllable count (final = main syllable).
2876.srule: Not mentioned in Sidwell & Jacq 2003 (sec. 4.2 'PWB phonological word' pp.33-34 and Oi profile sec. 3.7 pp.26-28 read; whole book consulted): the phonological word is at most a minor syllable + the stressed main syllable, and no secondary or rhythmic stress is described. 2878.dloc: Ch. 5, sec. 5.2 'Results of Experiment 2', pp. 48-49; supporting p. 21 and RQ3 pp. 80-81.
2878.prule: No stress rule stated. Tone language: the thesis tests Gehrmann's (2022a) five-tone hypothesis (possible mergers A1=A2 and B1=B2=D2) against a seven-tone hypothesis and finds 'evidence to support seven tones, with voice quality distinctions upholding the difference between /A1/ and /A2/ and between /B1/ and /B2-D2/' (abstract, p. ii; ch. 6 Discussion, p. 66: 'The results of Experiment 1 support Gehrmann's seven-tone analysis for Pa Then final syllables in citation form'); only B2=D2 is treated as merged (the five-tone categories are used only as the token-counting frame for Experiment 2, sec. 5.2.1); earlier descriptions of other localities give 7-8 tones. Only word-prosody statement: the author's auditory impression that the final syllable (right edge) of the word is prominent, non-final syllables and especially the presyllables ka, ta, ʔa, tə being prosodically non-prominent and reduced (iambic / right-headed, per the Hmong-Mien sesquisyllable literature the thesis cites).
2878.quote: Cross-linguistically, the edge of a word is a prominent position (Yip, 2002, 83). This is especially so in Southeast Asia, where iambicity is common (Michaud, 2012). In this context, structurally reduced presyllables are common, as are the diachronic processes that give rise to them (Gehrmann, 2022b, 6). Presyllables are common in Hmong-Mien, and Saxe (2021, 6) describes them for Pa Then. My auditory impression is that the right edge (final) of the word is prominent in Pa Then. Therefore, it is expected that the NFSs are not as likely as final syllables to bear the full realization of a tone.…

2878.exq_: Unlike ka, no evidence was found supporting the idea that ʔa, ta, or tə are different in kind from a NFS with /A1/ tone. (p. 81 - concerns presyllable status, not exceptions to a stress rule; no stress rule is stated)
2878.tone: Pa Then is described as a tone language throughout (thesis title: tonal contrast; Exp. 1 final syllables, Exp. 2 non-final syllables, Exp. 3 the presyllables ka/ta/ʔa/tə; finding: seven tones, A1/A2 and B1/B2-D2 kept apart by voice quality). On stress/accent the source says only that the word's right edge (final syllable) is prominent by auditory impression and that non-final syllables are 'prosodically non-prominent'; the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the thesis (0 hits in the full text). Instrumentally: positions are ranked 'from most to least likely to be realized fully... mono-, final, non-final, and presyllables. This was the expectation and most of the data fit it' (sec. 7.2.1, p. 77), but 'the falling pitch contours of /B1/ and /B2-D2/ are fully realized in normal syllables regardless of position within the word, their pitch fall is signi[fi]cantly reduced when they occur in presyllables' - i.e. ordinary non-final syllables realize tone fully with only co-articulatory variation (abstract finding b), and the pitch-fall reduction is confined to the presyllable ka (RQ3, pp. 80-81). The prominence claim is framed via Yip 2002 / Michaud 2012 iambicity, not as a phonological stress rule.

tn.quote: The tonemes of Paite is composed of minimal contrasting pairs known as minimal triplets and other tonemes conditioned by the presence of voiceless stop coda /p, t, k/ and glottal stop coda /ʔ/ to give rise to a total of five (5) tonemes in Paite. ... 3.7.1 Tonemes of Paite Word Tones Glossing a) /xa:/ M ‘spirit/soul’ b) /xa:/ LH ‘bitter‘ c) /xa:/ HL ‘moon‘ d) /xaʔ/ L ‘(to) let go’ e) /xat̪/ L ‘one (numerical)’
